\chapter{Los and Las --- Them, Derived}
\label{ch:pronoun-plural}
\hlchaptermodality{89}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can make any direct object pronoun plural, and say why the pronoun is tidier than the article.}

Complete ES-C45-los-las: produce los tengo and las hago, and explain why lo needed no repair in the plural when el did.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[los, las]{los and las — \textquotedblleft{}them\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C45-los-las}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Tengo el libro} becomes \emph{lo tengo}. Now: \emph{Tengo los libros}. Say the short version out loud \textbf{before} reading on.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: you were right}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{los} — \emph{them}, masculine. \textbf{las} — \emph{them}, feminine.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Tengo los libros.} $\to$ \emph{\textbf{Los} tengo.} — I have them. \emph{Hago las comidas.} $\to$ \emph{\textbf{Las} hago.} — I make them.
\end{quote}

Add \emph{-s}. That is the whole lesson, and you did it yourself in the warm-up.

Two chapters have now asked you for a plural and this is the first one that behaved exactly as you would guess. That is worth noticing rather than passing over: most of what is ahead of you in Spanish is like this, and the memorable exceptions are memorable because they are rare.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
There is one genuinely satisfying thing here.

The \textbf{article} could not do this. \emph{El} did not become \emph{els}; it became \emph{los}, because \emph{el} is a worn-down \emph{elo} that had lost its vowel and the plural had kept it.

The \textbf{pronoun} never lost that vowel. \emph{Lo} is \emph{illum} with the vowel intact — which is exactly why it was not \emph{el} in the first place. So when the plural came, \emph{lo} had nothing to repair:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{singular} & \textbf{plural} \\
\midrule
article & \textbf{el} (worn down) & \textbf{los} \\
pronoun & \textbf{lo} (vowel kept) & \textbf{los} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The two arrive at the same place from different directions, and the pronoun takes the plain road. An irregularity in one column and none in the other, from one Latin word, decided entirely by which one got leaned on.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}lo tengo\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}los tengo\textquotedblright{}; \textquotedblleft{}la hago\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}las hago\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el / los\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}lo / los\textquotedblright{} — one pair changed shape, one did not
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textquotedblleft{}I have them,\textquotedblright{} about books? (\emph{\textbf{Los tengo}}.) About meals? (\emph{\textbf{Las hago}}.) How do you make an object pronoun plural? (Add \emph{\textbf{-s}}.) Next: one more form, and it belongs to one part of the world.
\end{tcolorbox}
